message.content:
You are reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary as a BLACK BOX. The C++ library source is NOT available and you must NOT look for it.

Binary: /workspace/dataset/test20_executable
Invoke: /workspace/dataset/test20_executable '<word>'      (exactly one argument)
It prints exactly 20 lines to stdout, one per API call, in this fixed order (1-indexed):
  1  pluralize(word)
  2  singularize(word)
  3  camelize(word)                       // default 2nd param
  4  camelize(word, false)
  5  underscore(word)
  6  classify(word)
  7  tableize(word)
  8  humanize(word)
  9  titleize(word)
  10 dasherize(word)
  11 parameterize(word)
  12 parameterize("A " + word + " Test")
  13 upcase(word)
  14 downcase(word)
  15 capitalize(word)
  16 decapitalize(word)
  17 truncate(word, 5)
  18 demodulize("Test::" + word)
  19 to_string(isPlural(word))    -> "0"/"1"
  20 to_string(isSingular(word))  -> "0"/"1"

With no argument it prints nothing. With an empty argument it ABORTS (std::out_of_range from
basic_string::substr inside demodulize) printing nothing to stdout.

TOOLING TIPS
- Extract one line:  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable 'word' | sed -n '5p'
- Show exact bytes:  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable 'word' | sed -n '5p' | od -c
- Loop:  for w in a b c; do printf '%s -> ' "$w"; /workspace/dataset/test20_executable "$w" | sed -n '5p'; done
- Use $'...' bash quoting for control bytes / high bytes, e.g. $'a\tb', $'\xc3\xa9'.
- 'file' is unavailable; 'strings', 'od', 'sed', 'nl' work.
- The binary is fast; run HUNDREDS of probes. Be exhaustive, not economical.

GROUND RULES
- Every claim in your output MUST be backed by an observed probe you actually ran.
- Assume C locale: toupper/tolower/isalnum/isspace behave as ASCII-only; bytes >= 0x80 are
  unchanged by case ops and are NOT alnum. VERIFY this rather than assuming.
- Note operations are byte-based (std::string), not char-based. Test multi-byte UTF-8.
- Report the algorithm as precise pseudocode that a Rust programmer can transcribe with zero guessing,
  operating on BYTES.


YOUR ASSIGNMENT (humanize_titleize):
Characterize line 8 humanize(word) and line 9 titleize(word).
humanize hypothesis: replace '_' with ' ', then toupper the first byte. Check whether it also
  strips a trailing "_id" (Rails does): test "user_id", "id", "_id", "user_ids", "userid".
  Check whether it lowercases the rest ("aB" observed -> "AB" suggests NOT). Check squeezing of
  multiple underscores, leading/trailing underscores, trailing whitespace, empty-ish, UTF-8 first byte.
titleize hypothesis: capitalizeNext=true; for each byte: if c==' ' {push ' '; capNext=true}
  else if capNext {push toupper(c); capNext=false} else {push tolower(c)}.
  Verify: does it treat '_' or '-' or '\t' as word separators too? Test "hello_world",
  "hello-world", $'a\tb', "  spaced  ", "Foo::Bar", "HelloWorld", digits after space ("a 1b"),
  UTF-8 after space, and whether it underscore->space converts first.
Run at least 60 probes each.

apis.name: humanize
apis.pseudocode:
humanize(input: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8>

1. out = copy of input bytes (same length, always).
2. for i in 0..out.len():
       if out[i] == 0x5F ('_') { out[i] = 0x20 (' ') }
3. if out.len() > 0:
       out[0] = ascii_toupper(out[0])
   where ascii_toupper(b) = if 0x61 <= b <= 0x7A { b - 32 } else { b }
4. return out

NOTHING ELSE HAPPENS. Explicitly verified NOT done:
  - no stripping of a trailing "_id" (Rails behavior is ABSENT): "user_id" -> "User id", "id" -> "Id", "_id" -> " id".
  - no lowercasing of the remainder: "aB" -> "AB", "HELLO WORLD" -> "HELLO WORLD", "AuthorID" -> "AuthorID".
  - no squeezing of runs of '_' : "a__b" -> "A  b" (two spaces), "a___b" -> "A   b".
  - no trimming of leading/trailing whitespace or underscores: "  spaced  " -> "  spaced  " (bytes 20 20 73 70 61 63 65 64 20 20), "a_" -> "A " (41 20), "_a" -> " a" (20 61).
  - '-' is NOT converted: "hello-world" -> "Hello-world".
  - only byte index 0 is uppercased, even when that byte is a space produced by the '_' replacement or already a space: "_a" -> " a" (the 'a' stays lowercase), " a" -> " a".
  - byte-based, locale-independent (C locale): bytes >= 0x80 are unchanged by the toupper step: input C3 A9 63 6F 6C 65 ("école") -> C3 A9 63 6F 6C 65; input FF -> FF.
  - output length == input length, always.
  - all control bytes (09,0B,0C,0D,0A) are ordinary bytes, neither separators nor modified: "a\tb" -> "A\tb", "a\nb" -> "A\nb".

Note on the empty input: the harness aborts before printing anything when argv[1] is "" (out_of_range in demodulize), so humanize("") is not directly observable; the length-preserving rule means the guard `if !out.is_empty()` is the natural transcription.

edge_cases: Output length always equals input length (pure byte-wise map + single toupper).
Rails' trailing '_id' strip is NOT implemented: 'user_id' -> 'User id', not 'User'.
No lowercasing of the tail: case of every byte except index 0 is preserved verbatim.
Runs of underscores are NOT squeezed and leading/trailing underscores are NOT trimmed; each '_' becomes exactly one ' '.
toupper only touches index 0. If index 0 is (or becomes) a space, no letter anywhere gets uppercased: '_a' -> ' a', ' a' -> ' a'.
ASCII-only case op: bytes >= 0x80 pass through unchanged; UTF-8 multi-byte lead bytes are not uppercased.
'-', '.', ':', '\t', '\r', '\v', '\f', '\n' are all ordinary bytes with no special meaning.
Empty input is not observable (the 20-line harness aborts in demodulize); guard the index-0 write with an is_empty check.

apis.name: titleize
apis.pseudocode:
titleize(input: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8>

1. out = empty byte vector
2. cap_next = true
3. for each byte c in input (in order):
       if c == 0x20 (' '):
           push 0x20 into out
           cap_next = true
       else if cap_next:
           push ascii_toupper(c) into out
           cap_next = false
       else:
           push ascii_tolower(c) into out
4. return out

where ascii_toupper(b) = if 0x61 <= b <= 0x7A { b - 32 } else { b }
      ascii_tolower(b) = if 0x41 <= b <= 0x5A { b + 32 } else { b }

CRITICAL: the ONLY word separator is the literal byte 0x20 (space).
  - '_' is NOT a separator and is NOT converted to a space (no underscore()/humanize()
    pre-pass): "hello_world" -> "Hello_world", "a_b_c" -> "A_b_c", "_a_b_" -> "_a_b_".
  - '-' is NOT a separator: "hello-world" -> "Hello-world" (the 'w' is lowercased, not capped).
  - '\t' (09), '\r' (0D), '\v' (0B), '\f' (0C), '\n' (0A) are NOT separators:
    "a\tb" -> "A\tb" (the 'b' stays lowercase).
  - '.' and ':' are NOT separators: "a.b c.d" -> "A.b C.d", "Foo::Bar" -> "Foo::bar".

CRITICAL: cap_next is consumed by ANY non-space byte, even one that toupper cannot
change (digit, punctuation, byte >= 0x80). It is NOT "skip until a letter":
  - "a 1b" -> "A 1b"  (the '1' consumes cap_next, so 'b' is lowercased)
  - hex c3 a9 20 78 ("e-acute x") -> hex c3 a9 20 58: the c3 consumes cap_next
    (unchanged), a9 is lowercased (unchanged), then 'x' after the space -> 'X'.

Every non-first-of-word byte is LOWERCASED (this is a full re-case, not a
capitalize-only pass): "HelloWorld" -> "Helloworld", "HELLO WORLD" -> "Hello World",
"AuthorID" -> "Authorid", "McDonald" -> "Mcdonald".

A space always emits a space and re-arms cap_next; runs of spaces are preserved
verbatim and are not squeezed or trimmed: "  spaced  " (20 20 73 70 61 63 65 64 20 20)
-> "  Spaced  " (20 20 53 70 61 63 65 64 20 20). Output length always equals input length.

evidence.output: hex c3 a9 20 58 (c3 consumes cap_next; 'x' after space -> 'X')

evidence.input: hex e4 bd a0 e5 a5 bd
evidence.output: hex e4 bd a0 e5 a5 bd (unchanged)

evidence.input: exhaustive: all 253 single bytes 0x01-0xFF except 0x0A and 0x3A(aborts)
random: 499 strings len 1-12 over all bytes, + 400 strings len 1-30 over mixed ASCII/UTF-8 pool

edge_cases: Only 0x20 is a separator. '_', '-', '\t', '\n', '\r', '\v', '\f', '.', ':' are all ordinary bytes.
No underscore()/humanize() pre-pass: 'hello_world' -> 'Hello_world', NOT 'Hello World'. This is the biggest divergence from Rails.
cap_next is consumed by any non-space byte including digits, punctuation, and bytes >= 0x80 — implement it as a plain else-if chain, not as 'find the next letter'.
All non-leading bytes of a word are lowercased, so titleize destroys internal capitals: 'HelloWorld' -> 'Helloworld'.
Space runs are preserved exactly (no squeeze, no trim) and each space re-arms cap_next; output length always equals input length.
cap_next starts true, so index 0 is uppercased unless it is a space.
ASCII-only case ops: bytes >= 0x80 pass through both the toupper and tolower branches unchanged, so UTF-8 sequences survive byte-for-byte.
Empty input is not observable (harness aborts in demodulize); the loop naturally yields an empty string.

uncertainties: humanize("") and titleize("") cannot be observed directly: passing an empty argv[1] makes the harness abort (std::out_of_range from substr in demodulize) before any line is printed. Both models degrade to "" naturally; humanize needs an explicit is_empty guard before writing index 0.

Input byte 0x3A (a bare ":") also aborts the whole harness (out_of_range in demodulize with pos 8 > size 7), so lines 8/9 are unobservable for that single input. ':' inside longer strings works fine and matches the model ("Foo::Bar" -> humanize "Foo::Bar", titleize "Foo::bar"), so there is no reason to think ':' is special to humanize/titleize.
Byte 0x00 cannot be passed through argv, so its behavior is untested (irrelevant for Rust &str/String).

Inputs containing 0x0A shift the stdout line indexing; those cases were verified by reading the full numbered output ("a\nb" and "ab\ncd") rather than by sed -n 8p/9p, and both matched the model. Automated sweeps excluded 0x0A for that reason.

Locale was not explicitly forced; observed behavior is consistent with the C locale in every probe (no byte >= 0x80 was ever case-mapped, across ~3200 probes including full single-byte and multi-byte sweeps).
